opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of people frame real-robot data as a compromise. You'd love to do everything in simulation because it's cheap and scalable, but sim isn't good enough yet, so you grudgingly go collect data on hardware. I see it almost the other way around. Real-robot data isn't a stopgap. In many ways it's the thing that defines the problem.

The physical world has a long tail that's very hard to anticipate. Contact, friction, deformable objects, cables, cloth, the way a gripper slips just slightly on a wet surface. Those details aren't noise on top of the "real" task. They often are the task. If you only learn from a model of the world that someone wrote down, you inherit that person's assumptions about what matters. Real data doesn't carry those assumptions. It shows you what actually happens, including the things nobody thought to model.

There's also a scientific point. When you collect on real hardware, you find out quickly what your policy actually fails at, and that feedback loop shapes the research questions. A lot of the most interesting problems we've worked on came from watching a robot fail in a way we didn't expect. Simulation tends to hide those surprises, because you only see failures the simulator is able to produce.

And there's a scaling argument too. People assume real data can't scale. But if you look at what's happened with teleoperation systems, low-cost hardware, and many robots collecting in parallel, the cost per useful demonstration has dropped a lot. Once you have a recipe where more real data reliably gives you better policies, it stops being a practical workaround and becomes a foundation, the way internet text was for language models.

That doesn't mean simulation is useless. It's great for certain things, like locomotion, or for evaluation and stress testing. But for dexterous manipulation in messy, everyday environments, I think grounding in real-world data is the most honest way to make progress. It keeps you tied to the problem you actually care about solving.

r001.rationale: The response says real-robot data can scale through teleoperation, low-cost hardware, and robots collecting in parallel. It does not connect abundant data to robots eventually being deployed in people’s homes.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll complete the guest turn as Kay Ke.

Guest: Because I think the data question is really the question of what kind of thing a robot is learning to be. If you look at how language models got good, the data was already there, generated by billions of people living their lives online. Robotics has no equivalent. Nobody has been writing down, in a machine-readable way, what it feels like to grip a wet glass or slide a drawer that sticks halfway. That information does not exist anywhere except in the physical act itself.

So when people say "real data is expensive, let's use simulation or video," I understand the instinct, and we use those too. But simulation gives you the world as a physicist imagined it, and video gives you the world as a camera saw it. Neither gives you the world as a body encountered it. Contact, friction, the little recoveries you make when something goes slightly wrong, those are exactly where robots fail today, and they are exactly what sim and video throw away.

That is why I say it is more than a practical choice. It is a bet about where the bottleneck actually is. If the bottleneck were compute or architecture, I would spend my time there. But I believe the bottleneck is that the model has never actually touched the world. Real-robot data is the only way to close that gap, and whoever builds the pipeline to collect it at scale, cleanly and continuously, is building the thing that will matter most five years from now.

r001.rationale: The response argues that robot experience must be collected through physical interaction, but it does not say that robots will eventually be deployed in people’s homes or that home deployment will make real-robot data abundant.

astra-6.text:
I see real-robot data as a way of grounding learning in the consequences of action. A robot doesn’t just need to recognize what’s in front of it. It needs to act, observe what changes, and adjust when the result is different from what it expected.

Think about picking up a cup. Visually, that can seem straightforward. But whether the grasp succeeds depends on contact, friction, weight, and timing. Interacting with the real cup exposes those details—and the failures that tell you what the robot hasn’t learned yet.

So real-robot data isn’t just a practical ingredient for improving performance. It helps define what we’re asking the system to understand: how its actions affect the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses real-world interaction and learning from physical consequences, but does not say that deployment in people’s homes will result in abundant real-robot data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think real-robot data is more than a way to make a system work. It’s how we discover what the system actually needs to understand. When a robot acts in the physical world, its actions have consequences: an object slips, contact changes, something moves differently than expected. That feedback connects perception to action.

So collecting data isn’t just filling a dataset. It’s testing our assumptions about intelligence. Can the robot recognize that something went wrong? Can it recover? Can it use what it learned in a slightly different situation? For me, that makes real-world interaction part of the learning process itself, rather than simply the final place where we evaluate a model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses real-world interaction as part of learning, but does not say that robots will eventually be deployed in people’s homes or that this will provide abundant real-robot data.
